Its extended handle lets you glide it smoothly across the face, neck, and body, and practitioners and users regularly report support for relaxation, circulation, and nervous system regulation. rec2HifxMfwWHZPm8.Name: Craig Koniver

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Walking Away From The Prescription Pad", "body": "Koniver opened his Charleston, South Carolina practice in 2006 and describes stepping out of what he calls the pharmaceutical model, where the visit is spent managing a patient's medicines rather than the patient. He rejects the functional medicine label too, arguing it simply swaps pharmaceuticals for nutraceuticals and leaves people on thirty to fifty supplements a day while still treating this for that. He calls his own approach performance medicine, helping people perform at any age rather than chasing an abstract longevity target, and he tells Chance Garton that peptides, hormones and nutrients are a bridge, never the destination."}, {"title": "Cortisol, The Sun, And The Anabolic Night", "body": "On the architecture of the day, Koniver argues we are wired to be catabolic while the sun is up, driven by cortisol, and anabolic at night, when testosterone, growth hormone and melatonin take over the work of repair. He points to the stretch from 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. as the period of heaviest growth hormone output, says his clinic uses saliva cortisol testing across a twenty four hour period, and contends that cortisol also acts as a buffer against inflammation. Chance Garton hears the word itself as core and sol, heart and sun, a poetic reading rather than an etymology."}, {"title": "Eight Hours Is Made Up, Dreaming Is Not", "body": "Koniver is openly skeptical that anyone truly understands sleep, calling the eight hour standard elusive and made up, and noting that people in primitive times woke repeatedly to tend a fire and napped through the day. He suspects dream time may matter more than repair time. Chance Garton answers with his own account: his daughter, six months old at the time of recording, announced herself in a dream before his wife knew she was pregnant. Both land on the same complaint, that we are qualitative organisms living in a quantitative world of wearables, lab values and invented reference ranges."}, {"title": "Symptoms As Messages, Not Enemies", "body": "Both men treat symptoms as information rather than adversaries. Koniver says pain and illness are there for us, not to us, and goes as far as calling a cancer diagnosis the greatest gift someone could be given because of the correction it invites. He lays out five questions he works through with people, what am I, what do I do, how do I do it, who am I, and why, plus three biological temperaments he names self worth, self love and self safety. He links the self love pattern to worn out mitochondria and argues negative self banter takes a real toll."}, {"title": "Informed Consent And A Doctor's Own Emergency", "body": "Late in the hour Koniver describes the mitochondrial tools his practice is known for, NAD plus and methylene blue, framing them as the early tangible wins that give people confidence to think bigger. Chance Garton raises the criticism methylene blue has drawn online, and Koniver replies that he has found few negatives in his own clinical experience. Both then turn to informed consent, which Koniver argues no longer exists in medicine because patients are told only part of the story. He closes with his August 2020 hospitalization, which he frames publicly as the moment he felt closest to God, and with his refusal to franchise, wanting better rather than more."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dr. Craig Koniver is a true frontiersman of the coming age of independent and holistic healthcare. I've known Dr. Koniver for years now, as one of my best returning clients for biofield tuning, so I know he's truly hip to the mind-body-emotion synergy when it comes to health. But beyond that, he's also been a leader on the cutting edge for various treatments of the biochemical sort, an area that I have much to learn about, and I'm excited to share this conversation with you.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Food, Guilt and the Power of Belief", "body": "Craig argues that what people think about food matters more than the food itself, pointing to a study where Swedish and Thai women showed different nutritional markers depending on whether they believed they were eating their own traditional cuisine. He tells people to stop punishing themselves over cake and instead find sovereignty over their own subjective experience, joking he would rather someone love McDonald's than hate a kale salad. The conversation turns to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Tirzepatide, which Craig calls net positive for confidence and energy as long as patients get honest informed consent about side effects and habituation."}, {"title": "Peptides, Sourcing and Regulatory Capture", "body": "Craig walks through what peptides actually are, chains of amino acids under forty units that the body already makes, and argues they carry far fewer side effects than pharmaceuticals while still producing a feeling patients can notice, unlike most supplements. He explains that compounding pharmacies test for potency and sterility in ways offshore research chemical suppliers do not, and that the FDA pulled many tried and true peptides from circulation in October 2023. Chance presses him to confirm his suspicion that the ban was less about safety than about clearing the field so pharmaceutical companies could patent and control the market later."}, {"title": "Peptides, Performance and Latent Potential", "body": "The conversation turns speculative as Chance wonders whether peptides could be a lock pick for latent psychic ability, connecting it to how AI has unlocked his own creativity. Craig pivots to peptides and professional athletes, arguing that banning them from sport ignores that a supplement cannot substitute for the will and skill an athlete has already honed, comparing it to Lance Armstrong's doping documented in Icarus, where a doping amateur cyclist still finished worse than before. Craig insists this frontier is not about becoming a machine but about becoming divine, unlocking what is already innate."}, {"title": "What Diagnostics Actually Reveal", "body": "Asked what he would test first, Craig says hormones, especially testosterone, thyroid and cortisol, because balanced hormones correlate with a higher quality of life more than any other single marker. He is skeptical of standard cholesterol and inflammatory panels, noting that reference ranges are just derived from what is common in an unhealthy population rather than what is actually healthy. He does still value toxicity testing for glyphosate, heavy metals and mold, not from fear but so patients understand their burden. He describes reading intuitive signals between the numbers during patient conversations, saying the real medicine happens in the conversation, not the data."}, {"title": "Vocation, Peace and Everyday Mysticism", "body": "Craig says the biggest drain on health is occupational living, staying busy doing what is expected rather than pursuing a true calling, and that finding the courage to make that leap is the most important thing anyone can do for their health. He argues the highest achievement is not longevity metrics but peace, since real peace cannot be taken away once found. Chance draws a parallel between Craig's intuitive read of lab numbers and his own practice of drawing tarot cards, and Craig shares a story of sensing a patient's Adderall reliance was really an escape from a life he was not fully living."}]
